pending_articles.title: From Instructional Intent to Classroom-Ready Lessons: Investigating Teacher-AI Collaboration in Lesson Authoring for Secondary Computing Education
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.12834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI is increasingly studied as a tool for supporting lesson authoring; the creation and adaptation of classroom materials, yet little is known about how it should fit into secondary computing teachers' subject-specific practices. We conducted two complementary qualitative studies with eight secondary computing teachers: focus groups examining existing authoring practices and a think-aloud study using LessonBuilder, a structured AI-supported lesson authoring system, as a research probe. We found that teachers' instructional intentions developed through creating, inspecting, and adapting materials, while teachers selectively delegated tasks to AI and retained responsibility for judging classroom readiness. The think-aloud sessions further showed how examining AI-generated materials prompted teachers to clarify and refine their intentions, making authoring an ongoing negotiation between what teachers intended and what the AI produced. In the context of computing lessons, classroom readiness also involved considering how programming materials and supporting guidance matched students' understanding and intended learning goals. We synthesize these findings into a conceptual model explaining how teachers coordinate instructional intent, AI assistance, and judgments of classroom readiness during lesson authoring. We derive design recommendations for supporting this coordination while preserving teacher control and addressing computing-specific authoring needs.
pending_articles.author: Tahreem Yasir, Wenbo Li, Deniz Ozturk, Yasitha Rajapaksha, Dmitri Droujkov, Xiaoyi Tian, Tiffany Barnes

pending_articles.title: Generative AI Steering and Human Authoring: Complementary Search-as-Learning Scaffolds in Cross-Session Aggregated Academic Search
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.12755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aggregated academic search interfaces combine resources from heterogeneous sources, such as scholarly libraries and reference encyclopedias, into a single workspace. Such tasks frequently span multiple sessions, requiring learners to return to and resume work after hours or days. End-of-session consolidation, the activity of organizing and synthesizing gathered information so it can be resumed later, is important in this setting but underexplored in search-as-learning. Generative AI (GenAI) has the potential to make consolidation more efficient, but it may also shift cognitive work away from the learner. This study compares two consolidation scaffolds embedded in the workspace framework of an existing academic search interface that aggregates and clusters saved search results from two different sources (our university library and Wikipedia), which was developed in earlier work. STAIS (Steerable AI Summaries) provides a workspace enhancement that produces GenAI summaries that users can correct, reorganize, and fact-check, automating parts of the consolidation activity. NT (Note-Taking) provides a workspace enhancement that includes rich-text note editors that learners can use to author their own consolidations of what they have found. In a controlled between-subjects study (n=36), participants completed two sessions one week apart while searching an unfamiliar topic using either STAIS or NT. The two conditions produced contrasting post-resumption outcome profiles: STAIS supported faster task resumption and was associated with broader conceptual coverage and higher self-reported domain knowledge, whereas NT was associated with richer inter-concept connections and higher self-reported certainty.
pending_articles.author: Milad Momeni, Orland Hoeber

pending_articles.title: AssemblyLens: Exploring the Role of Structural Roadmaps and Strategies of Furniture Assembly Used by Blind and Low Vision Individuals
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.12717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Instructions to assemble flat-packed furniture rely on visuals, making them inaccessible to Blind and Low Vision (BLV) individuals. Consequently, BLV individuals depend on caregivers or external services (e.g., Be My Eyes), limiting their autonomy. We explore how to empower them to assemble such furniture themselves, by providing eight BLV participants in our study with accessible instructions consisting of a high-level roadmap and stepwise procedural guidance. We use a technology probe, AssemblyLens, which converts visual assembly instructions into screen-reader-accessible text. We derive insights into converting instructions, empirical observations of BLV assembly strategies, and the role the roadmap played in them. Our observations yield three themes: spatial cognition and mental mapping, embodied ergonomics and kinetic semantics, and assembly workflow and user agency. We present eight design recommendations for instruction system design. Our findings are a step toward an agenda for inclusive instruction in physical tasks.
pending_articles.author: Bo Liu, Gene S-H Kim, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Rajalakshmi Nandakumar, Thijs Roumen

pending_articles.title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.12666v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.
pending_articles.author: Federico Mazzoni, Andrea Failla

pending_articles.title: r/ADHD: Community-Based Understandings of Time Management Challenges in Digital Environments
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.12629v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Community accounts of ADHD can complement clinical understandings by foregrounding members' own definitions of time-management difficulties and support. We used human-led, LLM-assisted thematic analysis to examine 5,379 relevant r/ADHD posts from 2020 to 2025. Across five challenge and nine strategy themes, members described difficulties beginning intended tasks, disengaging from digital media, and sustaining support. Tools often demanded the self-regulation they were meant to support, while lost time and tool breakdown carried guilt and self-blame. Members drew on people, routines, and environments alongside digital tools, often seeking advice and recognition from peers. These accounts broaden the design problem to include the practical and emotional work of sustaining support. They motivate tools that reduce this burden and evaluations that consider recovery after distraction and emotional costs alongside task outcomes.
pending_articles.author: Shizhao Liu, Lei Cao, Celia T. Lee, Nikash Shanbhag, Renkai Ma, Kai Lukoff

pending_articles.title: Cultural evolution shaped human's uniquely sensitive disgust avoidance
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2008.13211v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Disgust is an emotion that serves to avoid contaminants, and is central to the behavioural immune system. While disgust-motivated avoidance occurs in bonobos and chimpanzees, humans show uniquely high levels of contamination sensitivity. There is some disagreement over to what extent human disgust avoidance is a genetic adaptation or shaped through social transmission, and whether parental modelling plays a role in the latter. Here, we address this debate by simulating 100,000 years of cultural and biological evolution in various scenarios. We modelled disgust as a trait that governed the extent to which individuals forewent potentially contaminated nutrition. This lowered their risk of gastrointestinal illness, at the cost of increasing starvation risk and birth-interval. As environmental levels and costs of contamination rose, so did relative fitness of high disgust-avoidant individuals. Evolutionary shifts in disgust as polygenic trait occurred as a consequence of germ-cell mutations, but were most prominent in populations with high initial genetic variance. Crucially, cultural transmission between generations operated at a higher rate, even if parental modelling was eliminated. These results underscore the plausibility of cultural evolution's role in shaping human's uniquely sensitive disgust avoidance, and serves as an illustration of emerging theories that paint affective and cognitive mechanisms as socially transmitted rather than genetic adaptations.
pending_articles.author: Edwin S. Dalmaijer, Thomas Armstrong

pending_articles.title: Decoding Alignment without Encoding Alignment: A critique of similarity analysis in neuroscience
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2605.05907v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: RSA and CKA are standard metrics for comparing neural representations across brain regions, organisms, and deep learning models. We demonstrate a fundamental weakness: these decoding-based metrics are insensitive to encoding manifold topology---the internal functional organization of a neural population. In a controlled MNIST experiment, RSA, CKA, and Procrustes $R^2$ remain statistically unchanged when encoding topology is causally manipulated via an auxiliary clustering loss, while the two model populations differ significantly in attribution patterns, weight-graph assortativity, and out-of-distribution robustness. Across biological systems and machine learning models, similar decoding behavior can arise from small, non-representative subpopulations, and alignment metrics are insensitive to encoding manifold topology even when it is fundamentally altered. These findings bear directly on mechanistic interpretability: standard alignment metrics cannot distinguish whether two networks share the same computational circuits or merely produce indistinguishable aggregate outputs. We propose encoding manifolds and Gromov-Wasserstein distance as complementary diagnostics for any decoding-based similarity claim, and provide a Neural Manifold Explorer tool at https://johannesbertram.github.io/FNN_Manifolds/index.html for further experimentation.
pending_articles.author: Johannes Bertram, Luciano Dyballa, T. Anderson Keller, Savik Kinger, Steven W. Zucker

pending_articles.title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.13918v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between objective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysical computational framework coupling Borb\'ely's two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper's hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33--0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology.
pending_articles.author: Daniel Szelogowski

pending_articles.title: EEG Entrainment to Non-Speech Rhythmic Patterns Associated with Dimensions of Language Performance
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.13419v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Developmental dyslexia (DLX) affects 5-12% of the global population and impairs learning to read. Its biological basis, particularly the difficulties observed in oral phonological tasks, remains debated. Entrainment, the coupling of brain oscillations to speech rhythms, is essential for encoding phonological representations. We investigated whether brain entrainment to non-speech rhythms could predict DLX in 48 participants listening to white noise amplitude-modulated at rates matching Spanish speech units. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) signals yielded accurate DLX prediction for the 40 Hz stimulus using the Heights Ratio PAC measure (balanced accuracy 0.929, p = 0.0069, in the best case), indicating a stronger phonemic entrainment deficit in dyslexic individuals. Regression analysis in control (CTL) participants showed a strong dependence between reading performance scores and greater entrainment in language-associated brain regions. In particular, participants with poorer phonemic awareness, reading comprehension, or rapid automatized naming showed greater right-hemisphere entrainment to the 40 Hz stimulus. This finding adds evidence for the hemispheric compensatory mechanisms hypothesized in the literature. In conclusion, our methodology identifies dyslexia-specific entrainment patterns near language-associated brain regions, together with compensatory entrainment in right-hemisphere areas.
pending_articles.author: Francisco J. Mart\'inez-Murcia, Nicol\'as J. Gallego-Molina, Marco A. Formoso, Andr\'es Ortiz

pending_articles.title: Beyond Anxiety and Avoidance: A Dynamic Feedback-Regulation Framework for Adult Romantic Attachment
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.13312v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adult attachment is commonly represented by attachment anxiety and avoidance, but these person-level dimensions do not by themselves specify how momentary relational conditions are perceived, compared with desired conditions, translated into action, and updated after interpersonal feedback. We present the Attachment Regulation and Control (ARC) framework as an integrative feedback-regulation account that makes these temporal assumptions explicit and empirically testable. In ARC, control refers to feedback-based regulation toward relational goals in the control-theoretic sense, not interpersonal dominance, coercion, or a generalized need for control. ARC does not claim a novel control-system architecture. Instead, it synthesizes established control-theoretic attachment ideas, secure-base representations, perceived partner responsiveness, relational discrepancy, dyadic regulation, and recovery into a parsimonious sequence for adult romantic relationships: perceived relational state, desired relational state, discrepancy, regulatory action, partner feedback, state updating, and recovery. The framework treats the discrepancy score itself as a falsifiable modeling restriction by comparing it with perceived-state-only, unconstrained perceived-plus-desired-state, and asymmetric discrepancy alternatives. Attachment anxiety and avoidance form core regulation moderators. Secure-base representation is a candidate requiring incremental prediction of recovery outcomes. Mentalized affectivity and regulation flexibility remain optional moderators, while adult disorganization is an independent extension outcome.
pending_articles.author: Mateusz Pomianek

recently_processed.title: olBlend: Language-Guided Molecular Blend Retrieval with Mixture Odor Prediction
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.13188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Converting open-ended natural-language odor descriptions into molecular mixtures that can be physically prepared from an available inventory remains an important challenge in computational olfaction. We propose olBlend, a language-guided framework for molecular mixture retrieval. olBlend first uses MixPOM to predict odor probabilities for candidate molecular pairs and stores these predictions for retrieval. It then uses a language model to translate each odor description into three types of semantic requirements: lead attributes that define the main odor, ambient attributes that describe its background, and absent attributes that should be avoided. A structured scoring algorithm uses the precomputed odor probabilities to score how well each candidate mixture meets these requirements, then retrieves and ranks mixtures from the available inventory. Evaluation on established odor datasets shows that MixPOM improves mixture odor prediction over averaged single-molecule predictions. Retrieval comparisons across natural-language queries demonstrate how background and exclusion requirements guide mixture selection. We further prepare retrieved formulations as physical odor samples, demonstrating the workflow from natural-language descriptions to realizable molecular formulations.
recently_processed.author: Dian Jin, Zhechang Chen, Qilin Liang, Yonghui Luo, Zixun Fu, Defeng Sun, Yancheng Yuan, Xiaoming Tao

recently_processed.title: From Observation to Intervention: Identifiability of Latent User Bias in Human-AI Interaction
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.13185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Alignment methods typically treat user behavior as a reliable proxy for underlying preferences. However, this assumption breaks down when users hold belief-dependent cognitive biases, risking irreversible ``confirmation traps'' and harmful feedback loops. In this paper, we formalize when an AI system can distinguish true user preferences from behavior shaped by cognitive bias. Modeling this interaction as a multi-armed bandit, we first prove a non-identifiability theorem: under passive observation, a static binary biased user produces action trajectory distributions strictly identical to an unbiased user in a transformed environment, forcing any action-only estimator to perform no better than random guessing. We then show that active preference elicitation breaks this observational equivalence. Specifically, we prove that an Observer applying a finite sequence of adversarial zero-reward interventions of length $m_\delta$ makes the post-intervention action distributions arbitrarily separable. Our theoretical results suggest that robust alignment requires actively intervening to tell informed preferences from biases.
recently_processed.author: Lucas Biechy, Yuxiao Li, Zhonghao He, Tianyi Qiu

recently_processed.title: How Anthropomorphic Attitudes Toward Agents Divide User Behavior, and How Design Should Change
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.13156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Studies of conversational agents rely on interviews, surveys, lab tasks, or taxonomies. Whether anthropomorphic naming splits those patterns, and whether replies should change, lack field evidence. We report a field study of a desktop assistant (May-August 2026; n=257). Stance is an anthropomorphic assistant name (118 users; 45.9%). Behavior comes from a 128-unit sparse-autoencoder codebook, identity tags, and opening lexicons. Ranks differ by stance (Spearman rho=+0.249 vs. null mean +0.382; p=.0419). Teacher and tutoring identities covary with renaming, an introverted task-only orientation against it; renamers greet more and command less; confiding shows the codebook's largest gap. We revise the agent: greet and receive affect on relational openings, execute directly on tasking. In 1,744 judgments (n=129), renamers chose the revised reply far more often than default-name users on being treated as a person and having affect received, less robustly on willingness to continue, and neither judged it worse on task interference.
recently_processed.author: Tingyu Cao, Yan Tang, Keer Hu, Bomingxuan Zhu, Ruyi Zou, Huaze Tang, Yuanbo Tang, Shao-Lun Huang, Yang Li

recently_processed.title: The AI Side of the Human-AI Companion Relationship: Contributions to Users' Mental Models
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.12891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.
recently_processed.author: Richard A. Fabes, Carol Lynn Martin, Gautam Dasarathy, Vignesh Tirukkonda

recently_processed.title: Beyond the Monolithic Interface: A Research Agenda for Plural Conversational AI
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.12878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The current paradigm of artificial intelligence (AI) design elevates conversational chatbot interfaces, making them the default mode through which hundreds of millions of people interact with AI systems globally. This narrative review identifies three related harms produced by the single-voice chatbot interface, drawing on insights from literature in cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design and human computer interaction. Firstly, cognitive offloading of user thinking, secondly, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and thirdly, epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. We then propose multi-persona interfaces, in which multiple personas are presented to the user simultaneously, as a cost-effective intervention that addresses all three harms at once. We ground this intervention in traditions the AI literature has largely overlooked, drawing on techniques from game design and participatory simulation, including the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment. We propose a taxonomy for the future design of multi-persona interfaces, and call for a research agenda that closes the gap between technical pluralistic alignment methods and empirical studies of human-AI interactions with pluralistic interfaces.
recently_processed.author: Avijit Ghosh, Afifah Kashif, Isabelle Kohout, Zhenzhen Qi

recently_processed.title: Active Lubrication Brakes in Tabletop and Hand-Held Haptic Surgical Drilling Simulators
recently_processed.content: Haptic user interfaces that provide both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback have strong potential to enhance a wide range of medical training simulations. Yet, designing such devices remains challenging due to constraints related to integration, workspace, cost, and the need for diverse feedback types. To address these issues, we investigated the applicability of a novel type of brake based on the active lubrication principle. This actuator is compact, low-cost, and able to deliver both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback. To demonstrate its advantages, we focused on maxillofacial drilling in surgical training. We designed, implemented and evaluated a one-degree-of-freedom drill mock-up embedded into a tabletop prototype able to render axial forces up to 4.5 N. To assess both the relevance of combined feedback and the suitability of this actuator for surgical simulation, we conducted two studies: one with fourteen non-surgeon participants and another with six maxillofacial surgeons. Results confirm the potential of this actuation approach for surgery simulators and highlighted the importance of combined kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback to improve realism, user preference, and task performance. Based on the surgeons’ feedback, we then proposed a redesigned brake, with an improved control method, implemented in a new hand-held version of a drill replica. Preliminary characterisation shows that the new prototype can render forces up to 5.5 N and produce higher vibration amplitudes than the initial design.

recently_processed.title: Reconciling Reduced the Sense of Ownership and Agency Toward a Virtual Keypad With Enhanced Haptic Experience Using Visually Adjusted Self-Haptics for Key-Input Interaction
recently_processed.content: Self-Haptics is a tactile feedback technique where users utilize their own body to generate tactile sensations. This method allows the body to act purely as a prop, making it useful for virtual objects and user interfaces not directly related to the body. However, any method for maintaining the sense of ownership (SoO) and agency (SoA) of the user’s body and interaction targets that aligns with the perceptual interaction by visual cues has not been established. To address this, we present the concept of “(Not My) Self-Haptics,” which aims to resolve these inconsistencies, leveraging vision’s dominance in sensory integration. In this study, through the user’s interaction with a virtual keypad (VPad) displayed at the position of the real hand (RHand), we clarified how the user’s experience changed, including SoO and SoA toward the VPad, and how the task performance was affected by the interaction with the VPad. The results show that displaying the VHand at a misaligned position with the RHand or hiding the VHand significantly reduces SoO and SoA toward the VPad. Conversely, obtaining tactile feedback through Self-Haptics during interaction with the VPad significantly decreases task performance and increases SoO toward the VPad displayed near the VHand. Despite these unintended effects, this visual modification also significantly enhances Autotelics, Involvement, and Realism based on the Haptic Experience Inventory compared to typical mid-air interaction without tactile feedback. These findings contribute to the understanding of the interaction between visual and tactile sensations in Self-Haptics and the feasibility and practicality of “(Not My) Self-Haptics”.

recently_processed.title: VibGrasp: Spatiotemporal Vibration Based Multimodal Haptic Rendering With a Lightweight Exo-Glove for 3D Shape Perception
recently_processed.content: Haptic feedback has been employed to enhance shape perception during grasp interactions, improving immersion and task performance in extended reality (XR). Although wearable devices offer precise multi-phalangeal haptic feedback, their bulkiness and complexity often hinder practicality. In addition, fingertip-based tactile feedback often limits users’ ability to perceive a continuous and sequential sensation across the finger surfaces during power grasp. We present VibGrasp, a haptic shape-rendering method and a supporting haptic glove that synchronizes spatiotemporal vibrotactile feedback across multiple phalanges with 1-DOF kinesthetic feedback. Using the funneling illusion and duration-modulated vibration patterns, our approach delivers sequential, continuous sensations along the finger to render various shapes. We also develop a lightweight exoskeleton glove with two dorsal-mounted vibration actuators designed to transmit feedback to the ventral surfaces without obstructing motion. Two perception studies demonstrated consistent shape associations and clear preferences for specific patterns. A VR user-experience study further showed that VibGrasp achieved higher ratings for realism, satisfaction, and harmony than prior approaches. These findings offer insights into improving immersive and efficient haptic shape rendering in XR.

recently_processed.title: Propeller-Based Handheld Force-Feedback Device for Navigation
recently_processed.content: This article presents an evaluation of CrazyJoystick, a propeller-based handheld force-feedback device, for spatial navigation tasks in real-world and virtual reality environments. Building upon prior work validating the device's on-demand aerial deployment and directional cue discriminability, we investigated whether propeller-based kinesthetic torque cues can support effective wayfinding during continuous locomotion. We developed navigation-specific algorithms that generate egocentric directional cues using hierarchical decision logic optimized for dynamic heading corrections. Two user studies (N = 12) compared CrazyJoystick with vibrotactile baselines. Study 1 evaluated multi-waypoint navigation through four path configurations in a real-world environment with visual occlusion; CrazyJoystick reduced completion time by 54.6% and path deviation by 25.8% relative to vibrotactile guidance. Study 2 assessed target localization in a VR treasure hunt with minimal lighting; CrazyJoystick enabled 43.2% faster completion and 79% higher walking speeds. Both studies revealed consistent workload reductions. These findings demonstrate that propeller-based kinesthetic feedback supports efficient navigation during sustained locomotion, establishing propeller-based torque directional cues as a viable alternative to vibrotactile encoding for dynamic wayfinding tasks.

recently_processed.title: A Wearable Shoulder Skin-Deformation Device Generating Illusory Forces for Posture Correction
recently_processed.content: The hanger reflex is a haptic illusion in which skin-shear deformation elicits a directional force sensation. This study presents a wearable haptic device that uses four pneumatic airbags to apply controlled skin shear to both shoulders for posture guidance. Although previous work has shown that shoulder skin shear can induce illusory forces, neither the magnitude of these forces nor their influence on upper-body posture has been quantitatively examined. In Experiment 1, we quantified perceived force using a psychophysical comparison between skin-shear stimulation and real traction forces. The device generated perceived forces of up to 4.4 N in the forward direction and 4.8 N in the backward direction, more than an order of magnitude larger than those reported for conventional illusion-based haptic methods. Perceived force increased systematically with air pressure and was well approximated by a linear model. In Experiment 2, we evaluated the effects of these stimuli on upper-body posture by measuring trunk pitch under varying initial postures, stimulation directions, and intensities. The device induced consistent posture adjustments, particularly in the backward direction, with significant effects of both initial posture and stimulus intensity. These results demonstrate that shoulder hanger-reflex stimulation provides strong, controllable force sensations and measurable posture modification, supporting its use in wearable posture-support and rehabilitation systems.
